To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the complainant carries a burden to (i) make a prima face case that its claim is correct and (ii) provide evidence to the extent that the respondent cannot reasonably dispute the claim.

(i) WTO panels have not developed an overall methodology regarding the burden of proof; (ii) WTO panels have committed errors regarding burden of proof in disputes submitted under GATT/WTO, SPS and TBT Agreements, and that (iii) such errors seem attributable to the absence of methodology regarding interpretation of key substantive provisions of the SPS and TPT Agreements.

(i) the burden to prove a violation of the TBT Agreement lies on the complainant; (ii) the burden to show the existence of a risk lies on the complainants in disputes under the TBT and SPS agreements; (iii) the burden to provide scientific evidence lies on the complain- ant in disputes under the SPS Agreement; (iv) the burden to demonstrate that the measures are necessary to achieve the objective lies on the respondent in disputes under the GATT/WTO
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following questions: (1) what is the burden of proof in WTO dispute settlement? (2) how is it allocated between the parties? (3) how is it discharged? (4) what are the implications of these findings for the interpretation of the relevant provisions of the GATT, TBT and SPS Agreements?
the question whether WTO adjudicating panels and Appellate Body are consistent and coherent in the way they allocate the burden of proof in cases concerning environmental policies.

the following questions. First, what does the case law of the WTO dispute settlement bodies tell us about the rules concerning allocation of the burden of proof? Second, what is the relationship of the case law to the rules on burden of proof in the GATT/WTO and the TBT/ SPS Agreements?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in the context of environmental disputes in the GATT/WTO, the party alleging a violation bears the burden to prove the existence of a violation.
, in environmental disputes, the complainant has to make a prima facies case that the measure at issue violates the relevant WTO Agreement.
in environmental disputes, the burden of proof rests on the complainant.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the case law of the WTO adjudicating organs has not provided a clear and coherent picture on the burden of proof in WTO cases, and in particular on the allocation of this burden between the parties.
WTO adjudicating panels and the Appellate Body should be more explicit about the rules of evidence they are applying.
WTO adjudicating organs have not yet developed a coherent and consistent body of case law regarding the allocation of burden of proving in environmental disputes.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the burden of proof in WTO disputes is not as clear-cut as it may seem, and that the current case law does not always reflect a clear understanding of what constitutes a prima facie claim, nor does it always reflect a clear allocation of the burden of proof.

the WTO system needs a methodology that would allow adjudicating bodies to interpret the substantive provisions in a way that is coherent with the general principles of burden of proof, as well as the general principles of interpretation.
the WTO adjudicating organs have yet to fully develop a methodology for interpreting provisions that may be relevant to environmental disputes.
